**LONDON, England (CNN)** — When HIV-positive Winnie Sseruma was invited to speak at the United Nations in New York last June, she never imagined that her health status would stand in the way of obtaining a visa.

Sseruma, who has been living with HIV for more than 20 years, was repeatedly questioned before being allowed to enter the United States. While preparing for her trip, the UK-based HIV coordinator for the charity Christian Aid discovered that the United States was among 70 countries worldwide that either banned or restricted entry for people living with HIV.

“I was told I needed to come to the U.S. embassy for an interview and bring a doctor’s letter stating I was fit to travel,” Sseruma told CNN. “At first, the embassy told me that the first available appointment for my interview would be at a date past the U.N. High-level Meeting I was meant to attend.”

Only after the United Nations intervened on Sseruma’s behalf was she granted an earlier interview date. She was relieved when her visa arrived in time, but the obstacles did not end there. Upon arriving at the airport in New York, Sseruma was detained twice for further questioning.

“It was so humiliating,” Sseruma said. “The immigration officers were asking me very personal questions about my health.”

A month after Sseruma’s ordeal, the U.S. Senate passed the reauthorization of President Bush’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), including an amendment to the ban on travel and immigration for HIV-positive non-citizens. However, the U.S. travel ban remains in effect and will continue to be law until the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) modifies its regulations. Fifty-eight members of Congress have sent a letter to HHS urging the department to take action.

Russia also imposes restrictions on travelers with HIV. Affected visitors are not permitted to remain in the country for more than three months. Anyone applying for a long-term visa must present a certificate confirming that they are HIV negative. A spokesperson for the Russian embassy in London told CNN that no changes to the ban were currently under consideration and declined to comment further.

Campaigning against these restrictions is **Ctrl.Alt.Shift**, a UK-based organization that seeks to engage young people in the fight against global and social injustices. The organization argues that there is no public health justification for “restricting liberty of movement or choice of residence on the grounds of HIV status.”

Are these laws outdated? What do you think? Tell us in the Sound Off below.

The fight against stigmas associated with HIV and AIDS has been widely embraced by the organization’s young members, many of whom are taking part in Ctrl.Alt.Shift’s protests across London. Last week, following two demonstrations at the embassies of Saudi Arabia and South Korea — both of which ban HIV-positive travelers from entering their borders — the organization held its third protest outside the Russian embassy in London.

“The level of proliferation of the HIV virus in countries that do not implement bans on HIV travelers is proof that these bans have no impact whatsoever, except for reinforcing the stigma,” said Neil Boorman, Ctrl.Alt.Shift’s project manager.

Boorman told CNN that such bans and restrictions further fuel the epidemic by driving the issue underground and forcing people to lie about their health on visa applications.

Tinchy Strider, a 22-year-old British rap artist, also attended the protest.

“I’m here because many young people are not aware of these issues, but if they knew these bans existed, they would want to do something about it,” Tinchy explained.

Eighteen-year-old Sian Anderson agrees. She believes that living with HIV is already difficult enough and that these regulations make life “even harder.”

“Some people are completely not at fault; they might have gotten the virus through blood transfusion, and Russia doesn’t take that into consideration,” Anderson said.

“Science has moved on from the days where HIV was an unknown virus. Now the world needs to move on too,” Sseruma said. “Stigma remains our biggest challenge.”

She was relieved when her visa arrived in time, but the difficulties did not end there. After landing at the airport in New York, she was stopped twice and held for additional questioning.

“It was so humiliating,” Sseruma said. “The immigration officers were asking me very personal questions about my health.”

One month after Sseruma’s experience, the U.S. Senate approved the reauthorization of President Bush’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, known as PEPFAR. The measure included a change related to the prohibition on travel and immigration for HIV-positive people who are not U.S. citizens. However, the U.S. travel ban remains active and will stay in place until the Department of Health and Human Services, or HHS, changes its rules.

Fifty-eight members of Congress have written to HHS, calling on the department to act.

Those seeking visas for extended stays must provide documentation proving they are HIV-negative. A spokesperson for the Russian embassy in London told CNN that no revisions to the restriction were being considered and would not comment further.

One group campaigning against such measures is “Ctrl.Alt.Shift,” a UK-based organization that works to involve young people in challenging global and social injustice. The group says there is no public health justification for “restricting liberty of movement or choice of residence on the grounds of HIV status.”

“The level of proliferation of the HIV virus in countries that do not implement bans on HIV travelers is proof that these bans have no impact whatsoever, except for reinforcing the stigma,” said Neil Boorman, Ctrl.Alt.Shift’s project manager.

Boorman told CNN that these bans and limits actually contribute to the epidemic by pushing the issue out of sight and making people feel compelled to be dishonest about their health when completing visa forms.

Tinchy Strider, a 22-year-old British rap artist, also attended the protest.

“I’m here because many young people are not aware of these issues, but if they knew these bans existed, they would want to do something about it,” Tinchy said.

Sian Anderson, 18, expressed a similar view. She said living with HIV is already difficult enough and that these rules make it “even harder.”

“Some people are completely not at fault, they might have gotten the virus through blood transfusion and Russia doesn’t take that into consideration,” Anderson said.

“Science has moved on from the days where HIV was an unknown virus. Now the world needs to move on too,” Sseruma said. “Stigma remains our biggest challenge.”

**HIV-positive activist faces U.S. travel hurdle amid protests over entry restrictions**

*London* — HIV-positive activist Winnie Sseruma has spent years urging governments to confront stigma surrounding HIV and AIDS. But campaigners say that stigma is still written into the immigration rules of some countries — including, until recently, the United States — complicating travel for people like her.

Sseruma, a prominent advocate living with HIV, has faced difficulties entering the United States because of policies that restrict or require special permission for travelers with HIV. Activists say the rules send a damaging message: that people with HIV should be treated as a threat rather than as ordinary travelers.

The controversy has drawn attention from **Ctrl.Alt.Shift**, a youth-focused campaign backed by the charity Christian Aid, which has protested against HIV-related travel restrictions and called for governments to end what it describes as discriminatory policies. Campaigners argue that such rules have no public-health justification and instead reinforce fear, misinformation and prejudice.

For years, the United States was one of a number of countries that treated HIV infection as grounds for exclusion. Under the policy, HIV-positive foreign nationals generally needed a waiver to enter the country, a process critics said was cumbersome, intrusive and stigmatizing. The restrictions also affected international AIDS conferences and advocacy events, with some campaigners and health workers unable or unwilling to travel to the U.S. because of the rules.

U.S. officials had defended immigration health rules as part of broader public-health screening, but HIV/AIDS organizations said the policy was outdated, noting that HIV is not transmitted through casual contact and that travel bans do nothing to prevent the spread of the virus. The U.S. later moved to repeal the HIV entry ban, with the change taking effect in 2010, after years of pressure from activists, medical experts and lawmakers.

Russia has also drawn criticism for its HIV-related entry and residence policies. Rights groups have said Russian rules can restrict long-term stays or residency for foreign nationals with HIV, and in some cases have led to deportation or denial of permits. Activists argue that these measures are especially harmful in a country with a significant HIV epidemic, because they discourage testing, treatment and openness.

Ctrl.Alt.Shift campaigners have used demonstrations and public actions to highlight the issue, saying that travel restrictions punish people for their health status and undermine global efforts to fight AIDS. Protesters have called on governments to follow scientific evidence and human-rights principles rather than policies rooted in fear.

Sseruma’s case has become a symbol for advocates who say the right to travel should not depend on HIV status. They argue that the real barriers to combating HIV are stigma, lack of access to treatment and discriminatory laws — not the movement of people living with the virus.

“Policies like these tell people with HIV that they are unwanted,” campaigners have said. “That is exactly the message the world should be fighting against.”

# HIV-Related Travel Bans Face Renewed Scrutiny as Activists Highlight Visa Denials and Discriminatory Border Rules

**London / Washington / Moscow** — International travel restrictions targeting people living with HIV are facing renewed criticism from health advocates, after campaigners pointed to the visa ordeal of Ugandan-born activist **Winnie Sseruma**, the long fight to reform U.S. immigration rules through the **PEPFAR** process, continuing restrictions in **Russia**, and youth-led protests in **London** demanding an end to HIV-related discrimination at borders.

Campaigners say such policies are medically unjustified, fuel stigma, and undermine global efforts to prevent and treat HIV.

## Winnie Sseruma’s visa ordeal becomes a symbol of discrimination

Winnie Sseruma, a prominent HIV advocate based in the United Kingdom and originally from Uganda, has often been cited by activists as an example of how HIV-related entry rules can block people from participating in major international events.

Sseruma’s experience drew attention because she was reportedly required to confront disclosure of her HIV status in the context of visa rules, a process campaigners described as humiliating and discriminatory. For activists, her case illustrated a wider problem: people living with HIV may be excluded not because they pose a public-health risk, but because immigration systems treat HIV as a basis for suspicion or denial.

HIV organizations argue that such restrictions discourage people from testing, seeking treatment, or disclosing their status. They also say the rules can prevent advocates, researchers, and health workers living with HIV from attending conferences where policy decisions about HIV/AIDS are made.

“People living with HIV must be at the table when governments discuss HIV,” activists have repeatedly argued. “Travel bans silence the very communities most affected.”

## U.S. reforms tied to PEPFAR amendment

The United States was long among the most prominent countries with HIV-related travel and immigration restrictions. For years, HIV infection was listed as a condition that could make foreign nationals inadmissible to the U.S., affecting travelers, students, workers, and migrants seeking permanent residence.

A major turning point came during the reauthorization of the **President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief**, known as **PEPFAR**, the U.S. global HIV/AIDS funding program. As part of the 2008 PEPFAR reauthorization, Congress removed the statutory basis that had treated HIV as an automatic ground of inadmissibility.

That legislative change did not immediately end the ban. The Department of Health and Human Services still had to update its public-health regulations. The U.S. HIV travel ban was formally lifted in 2010, allowing people living with HIV to enter the country without seeking a special waiver based solely on their HIV status.

Public-health experts welcomed the move, saying it aligned U.S. policy with scientific evidence. HIV is not transmitted through casual contact, travel, shared air, food, or ordinary social interaction. Effective treatment can also reduce the amount of virus in a person’s body to undetectable levels, preventing sexual transmission.

The end of the U.S. ban also cleared the way for major HIV/AIDS conferences to be held in the United States without excluding HIV-positive delegates.

## Russia’s restrictions remain a major concern

While the U.S. changed course, Russia has continued to draw criticism for policies affecting foreign nationals living with HIV.

Russia has maintained rules that can restrict long-term residence for people with HIV and may require foreign citizens to present HIV-negative certificates for certain visas, residence permits, or work authorization. Foreign nationals diagnosed with HIV have, in some circumstances, faced denial of residence or deportation.

Human-rights organizations and HIV advocates say these measures are punitive and counterproductive. They argue that deportation or exclusion based on HIV status does not prevent transmission and may instead push people away from testing and healthcare.

Russia’s policies are particularly significant because the country has one of the largest HIV epidemics in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Public-health specialists have warned that stigma, criminalization, and barriers to services make the epidemic harder to control.

Advocates say immigration restrictions should be replaced with access to voluntary testing, treatment, prevention services, and accurate public-health information.

## Youth activists in London demand change

In London, youth-led HIV and global-health groups have used public demonstrations, petitions, and awareness campaigns to pressure governments to end HIV-related travel bans.

Young activists have argued that the restrictions are part of a broader pattern of stigma facing people living with HIV. Their campaigns often connect travel bans with issues such as access to treatment, migrant rights, sexual health education, and the need for people living with HIV to participate directly in policymaking.

London-based campaigners have also highlighted the contradiction of governments funding HIV programs abroad while maintaining immigration systems that discriminate against HIV-positive people.

For youth activists, the message is simple: travel bans are not a public-health tool; they are a human-rights violation.

## Medical evidence undermines the case for bans

Global health agencies, including UNAIDS and the World Health Organization, have long opposed HIV-specific travel restrictions. Experts say such bans are not justified because HIV is not spread through casual contact and because excluding HIV-positive travelers does not protect the public.

Instead, public-health officials emphasize testing, treatment, condoms, harm-reduction services, pre-exposure prophylaxis, and anti-stigma campaigns.

Critics also warn that travel bans can have dangerous side effects. People may avoid HIV testing if a diagnosis could affect immigration status. Others may interrupt treatment while traveling or relocating. Migrants may be forced underground, making it harder for health systems to reach them.

## A shrinking but persistent global problem

The number of countries maintaining HIV-related travel restrictions has declined over time, especially after sustained pressure from HIV networks and human-rights groups. However, advocates say discriminatory policies remain in several jurisdictions, particularly for long-term stays, work permits, study visas, or residence applications.

The rules vary widely. Some countries require HIV testing for residence permits; others may deny entry, deport foreign nationals, or impose restrictions on employment. Even where short-term tourism is permitted, longer-term migrants can face significant barriers.

Campaigners say the remaining restrictions are often hidden in visa medical forms, residence regulations, or administrative practices, making them difficult to challenge.

## Activists call for global repeal

The cases highlighted by advocates — from Winnie Sseruma’s visa experience to Russia’s continuing restrictions — have become part of a broader campaign for mobility rights for people living with HIV.

Activists are calling on governments to:

- End HIV-specific entry, stay, and residence restrictions  
- Remove mandatory HIV testing from visa and immigration processes  
- Protect medical confidentiality  
- Ensure migrants can access HIV treatment and prevention services  
- Involve people living with HIV in policymaking  
- Base border and health rules on science, not stigma  

The U.S. repeal through the PEPFAR-related reform is often cited as proof that change is possible when political leaders, public-health experts, and activists work together.

But campaigners say the unfinished work remains urgent.

“An HIV diagnosis should never determine whether someone can cross a border, study, work, attend a conference, or live with their family,” one London activist said. “The world cannot fight HIV while discriminating against people living with it.”

# Are HIV travel bans outdated? Advocates say they fuel stigma, not safety

For decades, people living with HIV have faced barriers not only to health care and employment, but also to movement across borders. In some countries, an HIV-positive status can still complicate — or even prevent — entry, residency, work permits or long-term visas.

Public health experts and advocates say such restrictions are increasingly out of step with modern science.

Today, effective antiretroviral treatment can suppress HIV to undetectable levels, meaning the virus cannot be sexually transmitted — a principle widely known as “undetectable equals untransmittable,” or U=U. HIV is not spread through casual contact, shared food, air travel, workplaces or public spaces.

Yet some travel and immigration rules continue to treat HIV as a special threat.

## A legacy of fear

HIV-related travel restrictions emerged in the 1980s and 1990s, when fear, misinformation and moral panic shaped policy responses to the epidemic. At the time, treatment options were limited and public understanding of transmission was often poor.

But advocates say that keeping such rules in place today reinforces the idea that people living with HIV are dangerous — a view that is medically inaccurate and socially harmful.

Other nations have followed, though advocacy groups say restrictions remain in parts of the world, particularly for people seeking long-term visas, employment or residency.

Doctors say the scientific case for travel bans has collapsed.

**HIV Travel Rules Draw Scrutiny After Aid Worker Questioned en Route to U.N. Meeting**

*By [Reporter Name]*

When Winnie Sseruma, a UK-based HIV coordinator for the international development agency Christian Aid, arrived to travel to a United Nations meeting in New York, she expected the usual questions about her passport, visa and reason for travel. Instead, she says, officials focused on something far more personal: her HIV status.

Sseruma, a longtime advocate for the rights of people living with HIV, said the questioning underscored the stigma still embedded in immigration systems around the world. Her experience has become a stark example for campaigners who argue that HIV-related travel and residency restrictions are discriminatory, medically outdated and damaging to global efforts to fight the epidemic.

“This is not just about one traveler being inconvenienced,” said one health-rights advocate familiar with the case. “It is about the message sent to millions of people living with HIV: that they are a threat, rather than human beings with rights.”

Across the world, dozens of countries have maintained, or in some cases continue to enforce, rules that restrict entry, long-term residence, work permits or study visas for people living with HIV. Some require HIV testing for foreign workers, students or would-be residents. Others can deny visas, deport people who test positive, or impose special disclosure requirements.

Public health experts say such measures have little scientific justification. HIV is not transmitted through casual contact, shared workplaces, classrooms, air travel or public spaces. Effective treatment can reduce the virus to undetectable levels, preventing sexual transmission. Critics argue that immigration restrictions instead discourage testing and openness, driving people away from care.

Sseruma’s questioning while traveling to a U.N. meeting was especially striking to advocates because the United Nations has repeatedly urged governments to remove HIV-specific travel barriers. UNAIDS and other international health bodies have long said that restrictions based solely on HIV status violate human rights and do not protect public health.

“These policies belong to another era,” said a campaigner with an international HIV network. “They were created in fear, not evidence.”

The issue has long been politically sensitive. Governments that defend such rules often cite the potential cost of health care, concerns about public resources, or broader immigration control. But rights groups say those arguments unfairly single out HIV while ignoring comparable chronic health conditions.

For people living with HIV, the impact can be severe. Migrants may avoid medical treatment for fear that a diagnosis could affect their visa status. Families can be separated. Workers may lose jobs. Students can be denied opportunities. In some cases, people are deported to countries where treatment is difficult to obtain.

Christian Aid and other organizations have used cases like Sseruma’s to call for an end to HIV-based immigration discrimination. They argue that the global response to HIV depends not only on medicine, but also on dismantling policies that reinforce shame and exclusion.

Sseruma’s experience, advocates say, highlights a contradiction at the heart of international AIDS diplomacy: while world leaders gather in New York and other global forums to pledge support for people living with HIV, some travelers are still made to feel suspect simply because of their health status.

“The world cannot fight HIV effectively while punishing people for knowing their status,” said one advocate. “Travel restrictions do not stop HIV. They stop people from living openly, safely and with dignity.”
